props.title: Showgirls

sections.content: Showgirls (1995) stands as one of Hollywood's most notorious box office disasters, yet has transformed into a fascinating cult phenomenon. Director Paul Verhoeven, fresh off the success of Basic Instinct (1992), created this NC-17 exploration of Las Vegas showbiz that spectacularly miscalculated its intended erotic drama tone. Like The Room (2003) and Mommie Dearest (1981), it's achieved immortality through its excessive performances, particularly Elizabeth Berkley's aggressively committed portrayal of Nomi Malone, and dialogue so bad it becomes mesmerizing ("I'm not a whore, I'm a dancer!").

sections.content: The film's journey from $45 million disaster to celebrated camp classic mirrors other rehabilitated films like Valley of the Dolls (1967) and Beyond the Valley of the Dolls (1970). Verhoeven's other works, including RoboCop (1987) and Starship Troopers (1997), reveal his talent for embedding savage satire within seemingly straightforward genre films. This has led some critics to reassess Showgirls as intentional satire of Hollywood excess and the American Dream's dark side.

The film's influence can be seen in later works examining showbiz's seedy underbelly, from Hustlers (2019) to Black Swan (2010). Its explicit depiction of sexuality and violence, while gratuitous, broke boundaries for mainstream films. The movie's transformation from punchline to cultural touchstone reflects changing attitudes about camp, gender politics, and artistic intent. SUBHEAD: Legacy and Cultural Impact

sections.content: Showgirls' rehabilitation has spawned academic analysis, midnight screenings, and even the documentary You Don't Nomi (2019), which explores its complex legacy. The film's excessive style influenced drag culture and queer cinema, similar to the impact of Pink Flamingos (1972) and Whatever Happened to Baby Jane? (1962). Its memorable dialogue and scenes have become reference points in pop culture, referenced everywhere from RuPaul's Drag Race to academic film studies.
